title: Install smarter with selective installation for Value Accelerators
author: TillT
text:
Great news! 
 Selective installation in the Signavio Value Accelerator Library now lets you pick exactly the content you need from a Value Accelerator, and SAP Signavio takes care of the rest. Here is how to run one and make sense of your results. 

 If you have installed a Value Accelerator and found yourself scrolling through hundreds of diagrams, value chains, and dictionary entries that simply don't apply to your project, this post is for you. 
 Value Accelerators in SAP Signavio Process Manager are packed with pre-built, expert-curated content. But a full installation isn't always the right move. When your team is focused on a specific industry or process area, bringing in everything at once adds noise, slows adoption, and clutters the workspace your teams depend on. 
 Selective installation solves that problem. You choose the content that matters, and SAP Signavio automatically pulls in everything the selected content depends cleanly, efficiently, and with full transparency afterward. 

 To learn more about the the importance of selective installation of Value Accelerators, also check this short video . 

 Who can use selective installation? 
 Selective installation is currently available for SAP Signavio Process Manager Value Accelerators only. 

 Your three-step installation 
 Open the Value Accelerator Library, find the accelerator you want, and click Install in the top right corner. The wizard opens at step one. 

 Step 1 — Content Selection 
 Choose Install selection to activate the content browser. Use the search bar to filter by keyword, then click the plus icon next to any item to add it to your selection. You will see confirmation each time. Switch to the Selected tab to review your choices before moving on. 
 Note that, at this stage you will not get to know these dependencies. This content will be detected by the system only during installation run. 

 Step 2 — Customization 
 Select the content that is most relevant at the highest level and run the installation without the dictionary first. If the result meets your needs, you can delete it and redo with the dictionary included. This iterative approach saves rework and helps you validate scope before committing to a larger import. The full list of dependency-resolved content, everything the system pulled in to support your selections becomes visible after installation in the Installed content overview, so you will always have a clear picture of what landed. But first, continue. 

 Step 3 — Review and confirm 
 The final step shows a summary of what will be installed. Review it, confirm, and the system gets to work. You can track progress in real time on the Installed Accelerators screen. 
 In just a few clicks, you have scoped your content, let SAP Signavio resolve all dependencies, and track the installation through to completion. 

 Looking for more details? Check the step-by-step installation video . 

 Making sense of what is in your workspace 
 Once the installation completes, open the Value Accelerator Library and navigate to the Installation Log . You will see distinct status columns for each installation: one showing the result Completed, Failed, or Cancelled and one showing the type, either Full or Selective and one more for whether the dictionary categories and entries were included during the installation. Keeping these separate makes it easy to understand installations made within your workspace. 

 Click on any entry and a side panel opens on the right. From there, open the Installed Content Details overview to see every piece of content brought into your workspace, organized by type value chains, business process diagrams and more. within main content, or additional supplementing content such as custom attributes, and more. Critically, main content distinguishes between content you explicitly selected and content the system detected as a dependency. That transparency means you always know exactly what is in your workspace and why it is there. The view uses lazy loading and pagination to keep performance smooth even for large installations. 
 Folder-level visibility within this overview is planned for a future release. 

 This short video summarizes how to best work with selectively installed Value Accelerators. 
 You have now seen how to run a selective installation, navigate the results, and read the status columns briefly. Selective installation is one of the most effective ways to deploy accelerator content with precision, and your workspace stays exactly as focused as your project needs it to be. 
 Brought to you by the SAP Signavio Value Accelerator team.

title: Data Access Control (DAC) Scenarios in SAP Datasphere
author: abhimanyu_sharma
text:
This document demonstrates multiple Data Access Control (DAC) scenarios using different combinations of State and Category filters. Its purpose is to explain how DAC works across multiple scenarios and how access rules can be designed according to specific business requirements. Based on the requirement, permission tables can be created and DACs can then be defined using those permission tables. The cases show how single and multiple DACs behave, including OR and AND logic, unrestricted values, exclusions, overlapping access groups, and conflicting rules that return no data. Screenshots are included to illustrate each configuration and its result. 
 Implementation steps: 
 Step 1: Create the permission table. 
 Step 2: Create the DAC based on the permission table. 
 Step 3: Assign the DAC to the relevant views or analytical models. 
 I have not included detailed instructions for Steps 1 to 3 because they are already covered in many blogs on the SAP Community. This document assumes that readers working with SAP Datasphere are familiar with creating permission tables and DACs and assigning DACs to views or analytical models. 
 Refer this link for best practices : https://help.sap.com/docs/SAP_DATASPHERE/be5967d099974c69b77f4549425ca4c0/a032e51c730147c7a1fcac125b4cfe14.html?locale=en-US#loioa032e51c730147c7a1fcac125b4cfe14__section_best_practices 
 Note: As a best practice, create a dedicated permission space to store permission tables. Govern access by sharing the space only with the appropriate developers who are responsible for maintaining row-level security. 
 Dataset: The examples use the open Sales Data Set available on Kaggle. 
 Testing and privacy note: Each case was tested using a single User ID. User ID is hidden in the screenshots because they are personal information. 
 In Sales Dataset , we have state and Category dimensions holding data for multiple US states and multiple Categories. 

 Case 1: State = California or Alabama and Category = Furniture 

 To show data where State = California and Category = Furniture OR State = Alabama and Category = Furniture 
 Condition 
 (State = California AND Category = Furniture) 
 OR 
 (State = Alabama AND Category = Furniture) 

 SAC output 

 Case 2: All California Categories or Alabama Furniture 
 Condition 
 (State = California AND Category = *) 
 OR 
 (State = Alabama AND Category = Furniture) 

 SAC 

 Case 3: All Categories for California or Alabama 
 Condition 
 (State = California AND Category = *) 
 OR 
 (State = Alabama AND Category = *) 

 Case 4: Combining Two DACs on the Same View 
 DAC 1 ( Type Operator and Values ) 
 Condition : 
 (State EQ Alabama AND Category = *) 
 OR (State EQ California AND Category = *) 

 DAC 2 (Type Single Only) 
 Condition: 
 (State EQ Alabama AND Category = Furniture) 
 OR (State EQ California AND Category = Furniture) 

 Explanation: When two DACs are assigned to the same view, they are combined using AND logic. A row is shown only if both DACs allow it; therefore, the more restrictive DAC takes precedence. 
 Result: SAC will show California Furniture or Alabama Furniture. 

 Case 5: States from Alabama to California, Excluding Arizona 

 Requirement: User A should see states from Alabama to California, excluding Arizona 
 Explanation: The configuration below excludes Arizona and all categories associated with it. 

 Case 6: All States and Categories Except California Furniture 

 Requirement: Show all states and categories except the Furniture category for California. 

 Case 7: California with All Categories 

 Explanation: This is an alternative configuration in which the Category does not need to be specified explicitly. 

 SAC 

 Case 8: Overlapping Groups Without Duplicate Rows 

 Requirement: Show California with all categories, together with all states that have the Furniture category. 
 Explanation: Group 1 and Group 2 overlap, but the overlap does not create duplicate rows. 

 Case 9: Conflicting DACs Assigned to One View 
 DAC 1 ( Type : Single value ) : Show State = Alabama and Category = Furniture. 

 DAC 2 Type ( Operator and values ) : Show State = California and Category = All. 

 Result: If DAC 1 and DAC 2 are both assigned to a single view, no data will be shown. 
 Explanation: Each row must satisfy both DACs. DAC 1 allows only Alabama, while DAC 2 allows only California. Because a row cannot belong to both states at the same time, no rows pass the combined filter. 

 Comparison with SAP BW Analysis Authorizations 

 >Aggregation Authorisation in SAP BW 
 In SAP BW, aggregation authorisation using the colon (:) can allow a user to view an aggregated result for a characteristic without granting access to its individual values. SAP Datasphere DACs work differently: they apply row-level filters, removing unauthorised records before the result is aggregated. 
 Example 

 Cost Center 
 Employee 
 Salary 

 CC100 
 Mark 
 100 

 CC100 
 Bob 
 100 

 CC100 
 John 
 100 
 SAP BW result: With “:” authorisation for Employee, the user can run a query by Cost Center and view the complete aggregated value for CC100: 300. 
 If the user drills down by Employee, SAP BW blocks access to the individual employee values. The user can therefore see the full total without viewing the underlying salary details. 
 SAP Datasphere DAC result: A DAC filters out rows that the user is not authorised to access. If the user is authorised to view only Mark’s record, the rows for Bob and John are excluded before aggregation. The value shown for CC100 is therefore 100. 
 Key takeaway: SAP BW Analysis Authorizations can support aggregated reporting while restricting access to lower-level characteristic values. A SAP Datasphere DAC controls which rows are available to the user, so excluded rows do not contribute to the aggregate. A standard DAC therefore does not provide the same behaviour as BW aggregation authorisation. 
 >Key-figure (column-level) security: 
 SAP BW can restrict key figures through 1KYFNM, allowing sensitive measures to be hidden from selected users. SAP Datasphere DACs provide row-level security only. To achieve a similar separation in SAP Datasphere, separate analytical models may be required for different user groups. 
 >Hierarchy authorisations: 
 SAP BW supports authorisation at hierarchy-node level, including level restrictions, aggregated-only display, and hierarchy versions and validity dates. SAP Datasphere offers more limited hierarchy-based access control through DACs. 
 >Define once and enforce broadly: 
 In SAP BW, an authorisation-relevant characteristic is checked across the InfoProviders and queries that use it. In SAP Datasphere, a DAC must be assigned to each relevant view or analytical model. If a required assignment is missed, the data may remain unprotected. 
 Summary 
 SAP Datasphere DACs are well suited to straightforward row-level filtering at scale. SAP BW Analysis Authorizations are stronger where the requirement includes partial visibility, such as totals without underlying details, hidden key figures, or more advanced hierarchy authorisations, as well as strict audit and compliance controls. In a migration from SAP BW to SAP Datasphere, aggregation authorisations and key-figure authorisations require deliberate redesign rather than a one-to-one mapping.

title: Say goodbye to cloning policy changed time recording profile! Effective-dated Time Valuation is here
author: neethadevaraj
text:
Overview 
 Every HR admin who has ever managed time in a large, multi-country enterprise knows the complex challenges that comes with a single sentence in an email: " The collective bargaining agreement has been updated. Changes effective June 1 ." 
 What follows is a familiar scramble. You need to change an overtime threshold in your Time Recording Profile. But the profile is shared across thousands of employees. So, you clone it, rename it, update the threshold in the new clone, then mass-update Job Information records so employees are switched over on exactly the right date. Then someone asks: "What about the weekly timesheet that spans May 31 and June 1?" The Time Sheet is split and requires to be handled as part of payroll run. 
 I've heard this story from customers across industries — manufacturing in Germany, healthcare in Australia, retail in France. The pain is universal. The root cause? Time Valuations were not adapting to these changes themselves. A configuration object that calculates when people work, how much they earn, and whether rules are met — couldn't change over time without an admin/partner's intervention. 
 That's why we designed Effective-Dated Time Valuation solution. 
 At its core, the feature is versatile: instead of changing a Time Valuation and affecting all history, or cloning a profile to create a parallel universe, admins can now add a new time slice to an individual Time Valuation with a future effective date . The existing version stays as is for all past calculations. The new time slice is activated on the date it's meant to be effective. The hassle of creating clone of time recording profile, mass updating of Job Information and dual maintenance of time recording profile is completely avoided. 
 And this isn't just about overtime thresholds. The use cases span the full breadth of what Time Valuations do today: 
 Daily and weekly overtime rate changes - when a Time Administrator updates a multiplier from 1.5× to 2.0× 
 Night shift premium windows - when a shift agreement narrows the qualifying hours from 20:00 to 06:00 to 22:00 to 05:00 
 Break deduction rules - when a works council agreement changes the minimum break duration that counts against working time 
 Non-working day premium rates - when legislation mandates public holiday pay at 2.5× instead of 2.0× 
 Business rule conditions - when FTE eligibility for overtime expands from FTE <= 0.8 to FTE = 1.0 
 Health and safety alerts - when the threshold for a daily working-time warning moves from 10 hours to 12 hours 
 Late-arrival detection - when HR policy increases the tolerance window from 5 minutes to 15 minutes and adjusts the alert trigger from 2 to 3 occurrences per month 
 Multi-country configurations - when Germany and France share a time recording profile, but each has a rule change on a different date 
 And critically, the retroactive corrections . If an Overtime threshold was set incorrectly at 9 hours when it should have been 8, and this is discovered 15 months later via the Time Valuation Trace tool, the admin corrects the effective-dated slice for January 1, 2025. The system triggers a retroactive recalculation across all 15 months, for all the affected employees. 

 Configuration 
 The configuration model is intentional in its simplicity. Let me take you through the various scenarios of versioning. Versioning of Time Valuation 
 When there is a policy change, the admin navigates to the specific Time Valuation that needs to change — say, the `SPLIT_OT_10` Aggregate & Split Time Valuation that calculates daily overtime. Instead of editing the existing record (which would rewrite history), you add a new version with the effective date of the change. 

 For example: 
 Version 1 (original): Threshold = 8 hours, valid from the Time Valuation's creation date (01/01/1900) 
 Version 2 (new): Threshold = 10 hours, effective June 1, 2026 
 The old version is untouched. The chain of downstream Time Valuations — the ones consuming the output of `SPLIT_OT_10` — needs no reconfiguration. They simply receive whatever the versioned Time Valuation produces on any given calculation date. 
 This is the key insight of the design: you version at the point of change, not at the top of the chain . Downstream Time Valuations that are not affected by the rule change don't need a new version. Only the Time Valuation where the logic actually differs gets updated. Handling Cross-Boundary Timesheets 
 One of the most technically interesting aspects of this feature is how the time valuation engine handles a timesheet that spans a version boundary. Take a weekly timesheet for June 28–July 4, where the overtime threshold changes on July 1. 
 The system resolves the effective Time Valuation version per processing day when Time Valuation method is Valuate Per Day or Valuate Upto Today : 
 June 28, 29, 30 → Version 1 (threshold = 8 hours) 
 July 1, 2, 3, 4 → Version 2 (threshold = 10 hours) 
 The result is that the correct overtime is calculated for each day, even within a single submission. 
 In the Weekly Time Sheet, if the Time Valuation method is Valuate Whole Sheet or Period , the behavior changes. 
 The system resolves the effective Time Valuation version with Time Sheet or Period end date which in this case is July 4th. The value of end date of the Time Sheet is considered and calculated with the values as follows: 
 June 28, 29, 30, July 1, 2, 3, 4 → Version 2 (threshold = 10 hours) 
 Retroactive Recalculation 
 When an error is discovered in a system governing payroll, effective dating enables a clean correction path. 
 The admin updates the effective version of the Time Valuation that contained the error (for instance, correcting an overtime threshold from 9 hours to 8 hours effective January 1, 2025). This triggers a retroactive Time Valuation recalculation for the entire affected period. The Trace tool (Summary of Valuations) provides confirmation of the correction before a payroll rerun is triggered. No individual employee records need updating. No profile changes required. A single administrative action propagates correctly across all affected periods and employees. Attendance Quota and Effective-Dated Variables 
 It's worth noting how this capability intersects with Attendance Quota -- a feature that allows employees to request pre-approval for overtime, work from home, or higher duties. When an Attendance Quota Type is configured, the system automatically creates Time Valuation Global Variable Values for Attendance Quota Type "Overtime" (e.g., `DOES_QUOTA_EXIST_OVERTIME`, `TIME_SEGMENTS_OVERTIME`, `WEEKDAY_OVERTIME`, `WORKINGDAY_OVERTIME`). These variables are inherently effective-dated — they reflect the valid period of a specific Attendance Quota request. 
 This means effective dating operates at two levels: at the configuration level (the Time Valuation itself changing over time) and at the runtime variable level (employee-specific quota windows informing time valuation logic dynamically). Together, they allow a single Attendance Quota Type to serve many employees across different time periods without configuration duplication. 
 The system handles Time Sheets that straddle a boundary — if a weekly timesheet runs June 28 through July 4 and the Overtime threshold changes on July 1, the engine automatically applies version 1 to June 28–30 and version 2 to July 1–4, within a single timesheet for Time Valuations having valuation method as Valuate Per Day and Valuate Upto Today . 
 For Attendance Quota with variable `QUOTA_LIMIT_OVERTIME`, the Time Valuation method used is generally Valuate Whole Sheet or Period . Hence, the end date of the Time Sheet is considered for the calculation of the entire Time Sheet. June 28 - July 4 will use the version 2 values for all calculations. 
 Results of Time Valuation Trace 
 The Time Valuation Trace tool (Summary of Valuations) already provides a window into how time is calculated. Now, it provides the effective dated slices as well. 
 When a weekly timesheet spans a version boundary (e.g., June 28–July 4 with a July 1 OT change), the trace should clearly show two timelines : the calculation using version 1 for June 28–30 and the calculation using version 2 for July 1–4. For each processing day under a Valuate Per Day method, the trace explicitly states which threshold value was applied. 
 Payroll auditors, works council representatives, and HR business partners routinely need to explain to employees why their overtime was calculated differently within a single paycheck period. A trace that surfaces the effective-dated timeline removes ambiguity and reduces disputes. Time Recording Profile Visualization 
 The broader vision is a visualization layer within the Time Recording Profile that lets admins and HR compare configuration states across time. 
 With an "As of Date" control, an admin should be able to pull up the Time Valuation configuration as it existed on any date in history — and compare it to how it looks today, or how it will look after a future version activates. The visualization shows inputs, outputs, thresholds, and routing logic side by side across versions. 
 Limitations 
 Time Valuation method and type cannot be changed. This will raise an error that they have to be same for all effective slices. 
 Create Time Record doesn't support creating more than 1 time slice. 
 Inactive slices are not allowed and each Time Valuation will always have an effective date 01 Jan 1900 by default. 
 Attendance Quota type cannot be changed in time slices. 
 Best Practices for Effective-dated Time Valuation 
 Effective-dated Time Valuation should be used for policy and legal changes where minor changes in threshold, change in input or output time type group, raise messages, factor, etc. This should not be used to change the complete semantic like changing period results from monthly to weekly or visa versa. 
 As Effective-dated Time Valuation uses the end date for all Time Sheet and Period related calculations. Hence, it is important to ensure that you are getting the correct value at boundary conditions. For ex: For a Time Sheet period from June 28, 29, 30, July 1, 2, 3, 4, the calculation will be based on the July 4th time slice which is active. Kindly ensure you this expectation is communicated to stake holders as the results will change for the last week and will not be the same as other weeks when time slice changes on July 1. 
 How Can you request this as an early adopter? 
 This is an early adopter feature behind a feature toggle. You can request this by reaching out to us. You can reach out to us via your customer success manager, account team or directly to me via SAP community. You can drop me a message in community and we can get connected for this 
 Conclusion 
 Effective-Dated Time Valuation is one of those features that's hard to explain but immediately understood by anyone who has spent time in the trenches of payroll-adjacent HR configuration. 
 It doesn't change what Time Valuation calculates. It changes when configuration changes take effect, how they're managed over time, and what happens when the world doesn't cooperate with clean period boundaries. 
 For the admin who has been cloning profiles every time a collective agreement changes — this removes that entirely. It also now helps in adding new features with an effective date and don't require to worry about the recalculation that possibly runs for 1 yr or so.

title: The Autonomous Supply Chain is a transformation journey
author: martin_stocker
text:
Executive summary 
 On Sept 24th, we kicked off our webinar series on SAP Signavio and SAP Extended Warehouse Management (EWM) with the session “ The Autonomous Supply Chain Isn’t a Destination — It’s a Transformation Capability .” SAP experts Gunther Sanchez, Timm Hemmert, and Dominik Lehmann shared how supply chain leaders can move from reactive, siloed operations toward a more connected, AI-enabled operating model. 
 The key message was clear: volatility is now the baseline. Demand uncertainty, trade disruptions, rising costs, and higher customer expectations are putting traditional supply chain models under pressure. AI can help, but the starting point is process transparency — understanding where value is trapped, where bottlenecks occur, and where improvement efforts will have the greatest impact.

title: Wrong ABAP documentation for NEW-PAGE Obsolete Specification of Spool Parameters
author: Sandra_Rossi
text:
Obsolete Specification of Spool Parameters - ABAP Keyword Documentation 
 "flag expects a single-character text field, where a blank character activates the parameter and any other character deactivates the parameter." 
 I think it should be the opposite: 
 "flag expects a single-character text field, where a blank character deactivates the parameter and any other character activates the parameter." 
 For instance, the following means that the spool is sent immediately to the output device: NEW-PAGE PRINT ON DESTINATION 'LOCL' IMMEDIATELY 'X' KEEP IN SPOOL 'X' NO DIALOG. 
 For information, in German it's the same assertion as English: "Für flag muss ein einstelliges Textfeld angegeben werden, wobei ein Leerzeichen den Parameter ein- und ein anderes Zeichen den Parameter ausschaltet." 
 I posted a feedback to SAP, I'll update this thread when I get an answer. 
 Thanks. 
 Sandra

title: How can I populate the Applications column in Solution Process Analysis?
author: davi3
text:
Hello SAP Community, 
 In the Solution Process Analysis app, there is an Applications column. However, this column always displays 0 for all solution processes. 
 The processes in our project are standard processes associated with SAP scope items. I could not find an option to assign applications directly to these standard processes. 
 We need to populate our scope items or solution processes with their corresponding applications so that this information is displayed correctly in the Solution Process Analysis app. 
 Could you please clarify: 

 How is the Applications column populated? 

 Is this information automatically derived from SAP Best Practices content or from the applications associated with each scope item? 

 Is it possible to assign applications to standard solution processes? 

 If direct assignment is not possible, do we need to copy the standard process and create a custom process? 

 Are there any prerequisites or configurations required for the applications to appear in this analysis? 
 Thank you in advance for your support.

title: Onboarding additional data - How does HR review after it's entered
author: Jen_Cooper
text:
Hi 
 In our process the onboardee needs to show proof of education information and upload a document that shows proof of their education. Where can an HR user review that information before manage pending hires is performed? 
 Do they need to go to the onboarding dashboard look up the employee and review the information there ? 
 Is there any best practice to use so it's recorded HR has reviewed this document? 
 Just want to make sure this is as streamlined as possible for our users.
